tells: Plain exposition that reports the Sheikh's qualification ('Sheikh Bahmanpour is careful about what this means') and leaves out the comma before 'and', as in the reference ('They think not about themselves but about God and in their hearts...').
'So the believers of this verse are believers who know Allah' - Author A never opens a sentence with 'So'; would write 'The believers of this verse are thus the believers who know Allah'.
'Sheikh Bahmanpour puts it simply: there are two groups' - a framing claim, then a colon, then the point; Author A states it directly: 'Sheikh Bahmanpour divides people into two groups'.
'The Qur'an describes them repeatedly' / 'asks about ordinary believers' - looser word choice than Author A's measured 'more than once' / 'looks at'.
'A heart only trembles' - misplaced 'only'; Author A is exact in placement ('trembles only').

Short reporting sentences ('Sheikh Bahmanpour says this kind of mysticism must be held apart from the real thing'), and the quotation is glossed and then closed with a plain definition. There is no editorial flourish.

The inserted 'he says' reporting matches the reference ('In most of us, he says, it is not working'). The closing paragraph restates the chapter's case in plain declaratives, as the reference does with 'Four times in a row, the Qur'an makes the same point'.

'It is the patience of a heart that has done its part and leaves the rest to God, whose light never stops' - a lyrical, aphoristic paragraph close; Author A glosses a quotation plainly and stops, e.g. 'He adds that this is not easy and requires a great deal of training'.
'The waiting is not for a light that is absent' - a devotional, warmer register than Author A's sober exposition.

The paragraph picks up the previous image and the next sentence of the source ('The next sentence of the oration gives the reason'), and the quotation is followed by a plain analytic gloss ('each statement says what God is not and none says what He is').

The opening picks up the previous chapter step ('If the faculty can be repaired'), as in the reference ('Placing the fault in the receiver has two consequences'). It uses 'thus' rather than an opening 'So', and the paragraph links forward to the next verse.

Each scholar's quotation is introduced by name and spoken to, then the paragraph ends on a reasoned inference ('If even Paradise is not to be the goal, powers certainly are not'), like 'If the signs are present and plain... the fault is on our side'. The one oddity is 'the lecturer's own word' where the reference says 'the Sheikh'.
Plain definitional sentences, a worked everyday example and short closing sentences ('They cannot be wrong that they feel hungry'). This matches the reference's red-light and machine explanations.
'The answer to how God can be known lies in a soul we have hardly begun to know' - a tidy wordplay aphorism as the paragraph's last line; Author A ends on the Sheikh's claim or a plain consequence.
'The soul is not an empty place to look' - a figurative, slightly gnomic opener; Author A opens by picking up the previous point in literal terms ('Repair is only the start').

'Sheikh Bahmanpour reads this verse as naming four ranks...' matches the reference's 'Sheikh Bahmanpour reads it as being about...', and the gloss works through the verse step by step. The stray 'The access.' looks like residue from a stripped heading, not a mark of another hand.
'Shirk, associating partners with God, is the gravest charge in Islam and he does not soften it' - an added editorial comment at the paragraph's end; Author A would stop at the definition.
'about something else: catching the signs of Allah: becoming sensitive' - two colons stacked in one sentence; Author A uses one colon per sentence.
'for very different reasons' - an intensifier Author A avoids; would write 'for different reasons'.
'Sheikh Bahmanpour opened his course by pointing out that people take up...' - wordy reporting frame; Author A states the point and attributes it briefly ('Sheikh Bahmanpour says').
